excerpt: Open a local project folder in Kimi Code Desktop and let the Agent read code, edit files, run commands, and verify results through conversation.
Chat with AI in the terminal, letting it read code, edit files, execute commands, search the web, and autonomously complete development tasks.
run `kimi` in the terminal to start; on first use, log in to the Kimi Code platform with the `/login` command to complete the connection — no need to manually manage an API Key.
Collaborate with AI in the editor sidebar, supporting code completion, file editing, web search, and automated tasks.
Other editors such as JetBrains and Zed can connect via CLI's ACP protocol.
A million-token context loads an entire large codebase with cross-module dependencies in one pass, enabling whole-project understanding and refactoring.
Choose between the standard K2.8 Preview and the K2.7 Code HighSpeed tier, with output up to 260 tokens/s for a noticeably faster coding loop.
supports `low` / `high` / `max` thinking effort levels. Best for large codebase analysis, multi-file refactoring, and long-document processing.
Compatible with Kimi Code CLI, Claude Code, VS Code, and other mainstream agent tools — switch models seamlessly.
The Kimi Code API is compatible with both OpenAI and Anthropic protocols.
Kimi members can create and manage API Keys in the Kimi Code Console (up to 5 keys; each is shown only once upon creation—please keep it safe).
An easy-to-use, stable, and cost-effective LLM API service for developers and enterprises, helping AI applications move quickly from development to deployment and scale.

K3 API pricing of $3/$15 per 1M tokens is called extremely high for a Chinese open-weight model, matching Sonnet. The commenter warns heavy reasoning-token use could make it costlier in practice than reasoning-efficient GPT models.
One user observed that K3 seems to use only about 60% as many reasoning tokens as K2.6, so the price hike is not as bad as it looks.
A user found that K3 seems to have kept the K2 series' creative writing abilities, at least with the prompts they had tested so far.
Complaint: account creation is only possible with a phone number or a Google account, which the user called lame.
"Not worth it. I have just tried a single prompt in the web interface and it is still not finish reasoning. It thinks too much and often repeats the same stuff over and over."
A user with a free GitHub Copilot quota says Kimi K2.7 is the model they are most happy with among those available, given its cost/performance.

K3 API parameters are inflexible: reasoning_effort supports only "max" with thinking always on, temperature/top_p are fixed, vision input doesn't accept public image URLs, and web search isn't recommended for production.

On a Tiananmen Square test via kimi.com, K2 without Thinking refused: "I can't provide information on this topic." With Thinking on, it pulled from Wikipedia and described the 1989 protests and estimated death tolls.
"The non-thinking version is the best writer by far." The user says Moonshot "really cooked" something different from other frontier labs.
K2 Thinking was the only recent model that gave a human-like solution to the egg/object stacking problem on the first try.
Praise for K3 versus Fable: "A third the cost, open source, and won't refuse every other request because of some vague possible connection to cybersecurity concerns."
A DeepSeek user says Kimi K3 now offers a great planning assistant for more advanced coding tasks (Rust, PSQL, Angular, Terraform).
In FastAPI/Spring Boot tasks, GLM-5.2 and Kimi spend roughly 70–80K tokens grepping the codebase before writing anything, then typically break the code. The user says Qwen3.7-Max "just… does it."
Skeptic citing arena.ai: Fable 5 dominates almost every category, while Kimi K3 has an edge in WebDev but struggles to reach the top 10 in many others.
Trialing K2.6 through a work subscription: "so far it looks on par, if not better, than opus."
"I've always been surprised Kimi doesn't get more attention than it does. It's always stood out to me in terms of creativity, quality... has been my favorite model for awhile."
Kimi 2.5 was really good for design but borderline useless on backend/advanced tasks; using OpenCode instead of the Kimi CLI really hurt performance.
Running K2.6 through OpenCode to Kimi's API, it "overthinks": pages of thought, 50k+ output tokens going in circles without doing anything — complete analysis paralysis.

In one user's tests, K2.6 did only slightly better than K2.5, struggling with puzzle and trick-style exactness tasks with frequent instruction misses. Probably a great coding model, but less intelligent overall than SOTA.
K2.6 couldn't solve the user's mixed-up wolf/goat/cabbage puzzle. Sonnet 4.6 also failed, while Opus 4.7 had no problems.
